denomProfiles/russian-orthodox-outside-r: Émigré Russian Orthodox church, self-governing within the Moscow Patriarchate since 2007.
Holds the full Eastern Orthodox faith of the seven Ecumenical Councils.
Originated under Patriarch Tikhon's 1920 decree allowing cut-off dioceses to govern themselves.
Rejected Metropolitan Sergius's 1927 declaration of loyalty to the Soviet state.
Canonised the New Martyrs and Confessors of Russia, including the imperial family, in 1981.
Since the 2007 Act of Canonical Communion it is a self-governing part of the Russian Orthodox Church.
Preserving Russian Orthodox tradition in emigration.
Strict liturgical and ascetic traditionalism.
Monastic life, especially Holy Trinity Monastery in Jordanville, New York.
Mission among Western converts in English and other languages.
Keeps the Julian calendar.
Byzantine liturgy in Church Slavonic, with English, German and other languages in the diaspora.
Governed by a Synod of Bishops based in New York and led by a First Hierarch.
Venerates John Maximovitch of Shanghai and San Francisco (canonised 1994).
Western convert Orthodoxy
Writers such as Seraphim Rose drew many Western converts to traditional Orthodoxy.
Russian Orthodox Church
Its canonisation of the New Martyrs influenced the Moscow Patriarchate's own canonisation in 2000.
Anthony (Khrapovitsky)
First head of the synod abroad (1920–36).
John (Maximovitch)
Archbishop of Shanghai and San Francisco, canonised in 1994.
Seraphim Rose
American convert monk and writer of the Platina monastery.
Laurus (Škurla)
First Hierarch who signed the 2007 Act of Canonical Communion.
denomProfiles/oriental-orthodox/tagline: Ancient non-Chalcedonian churches confessing one incarnate nature of God the Word.
denomProfiles/oriental-orthodox/coreDoct: Accept the first three Ecumenical Councils (Nicaea 325, Constantinople 381, Ephesus 431) and reject Chalcedon (451).
Confess Christ's single united divine-human nature, following Cyril's formula 'one incarnate nature of God the Word' (miaphysitism).
Reject both Nestorianism and the Eutychian view that Christ's humanity was absorbed into his divinity.
Joint statements with the Eastern Orthodox (1989–90) and Catholic common declarations agree that the differences are largely terminological.
Hold Holy Tradition and the Fathers as authoritative alongside Scripture.
denomProfiles/oriental-orthodox/focuses/: Survival of ancient Christian communities in Egypt, Syria, Armenia, Ethiopia, Eritrea and India.
Monasticism and fasting as central disciplines.
Preservation of ancient liturgical languages: Coptic, Syriac, Classical Armenian and Ge'ez.
Ecumenical dialogue with Eastern Orthodox and Catholics.
denomProfiles/oriental-orthodox/practice: Six autocephalous churches (Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopian, Eritrean and Malankara) in communion but without a single head.
Ancient liturgies such as those of St Basil, St James and the Armenian Badarak.
Infants receive baptism, chrismation and Communion together.
Strict and frequent fasting, often abstaining from all animal products.
denomProfiles/oriental-orthodox/influenc: Syriac Orthodox bishop Gregorios Abdul Jaleel's arrival in 1665 linked Indian St Thomas Christians to the Syriac Orthodox Church.
Coptic, Syriac, Armenian and Ethiopian Catholic churches separated from them.
Their dialogues helped clarify that Chalcedonians and non-Chalcedonians share the same faith in substance.
denomProfiles/oriental-orthodox/keyFigur: Theologian of the one incarnate nature.
Patriarch deposed at Chalcedon, honoured as a saint by the Copts.
6th-century bishop who ordained a separate hierarchy across Syria.
denomProfiles/oriental-orthodox/inIndia: Kerala's Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church and Jacobite Syrian Christian Church, heirs of the St Thomas Christians, are the main Oriental Orthodox churches in India, alongside a small Armenian presence in Kolkata and Chennai.
denomProfiles/coptic-orthodox/tagline: Egypt's ancient church of St Mark, mother of monasticism.
denomProfiles/coptic-orthodox/coreDoctri: Holds the miaphysite Christology of Cyril of Alexandria and rejects the Council of Chalcedon.
Claims apostolic foundation by Mark the Evangelist; its head is the Pope of Alexandria.
Accepts the first three Ecumenical Councils and seven sacraments.
Teaches that salvation is received through faith, the sacraments and a life of repentance and good works.
Venerates the martyrs and the Virgin Mary; Marian apparitions such as Zeitoun (1968) are widely honoured.
denomProfiles/coptic-orthodox/focuses/0: The monastic heritage of Antony, Pachomius and the Desert Fathers, renewed by a 20th-century monastic revival.
denomProfiles/coptic-orthodox/focuses/1: Sunday schools and religious education, from Habib Girgis's movement (1918).
denomProfiles/coptic-orthodox/focuses/2: Martyrdom and endurance amid sectarian violence in Egypt and Libya.
denomProfiles/coptic-orthodox/focuses/3: Care for a growing worldwide diaspora.
denomProfiles/coptic-orthodox/practices/: Liturgies of St Basil, St Gregory and St Cyril in Coptic and Arabic, with cymbals and triangles.
Uses the Coptic calendar, counting years from the Era of the Martyrs (AD 284).
Very extensive fasting: over 200 days a year without animal products.
Many Copts bear a small cross tattoo on the wrist.
Pope Shenouda III (1971–2012) and Pope Tawadros II (since 2012) have led a period of expansion.
denomProfiles/coptic-orthodox/influenced: Ethiopia's metropolitans were Egyptian monks sent by Alexandria until 1959.
A Catholic branch separated in the 18th century.
Through John Cassian and others, Egyptian monastic teaching shaped Benedictine and wider Western monastic life.
denomProfiles/coptic-orthodox/keyFigures: Traditional founder and first bishop of Alexandria.
Theologian of the Council of Ephesus.
Pope (1971–2012) who expanded the church's education and diaspora.
denomProfiles/ethiopian-orthodox-tewahed: Africa's ancient Christian kingdom church, keeping Ge'ez worship and the tabot.
Tewahedo ('made one') expresses the miaphysite faith in the one united nature of Christ.
Accepts the first three Ecumenical Councils and rejects Chalcedon.
Has the broadest biblical canon in Christianity, often counted as 81 books, including 1 Enoch and Jubilees.
Keeps some Old Testament observances, such as both Sabbath and Sunday, circumcision and dietary laws, as part of its tradition.
Honours the Virgin Mary and the saints intensely, with many monthly feasts.
Worship and chant, with the zema chant ascribed to St Yared.
Monasticism and church schools that train priests and debtera (lay scholar-singers).
Ethiopian national and cultural identity.
Fasting and pilgrimage, especially to Lalibela and Aksum.
Every church has a tabot, a consecrated altar tablet representing the Ark of the Covenant.
Liturgy in Ge'ez, with increasing use of Amharic and other languages.
Fasts about 180–250 days a year, depending on the person's status.
Great festivals such as Timket (Epiphany) and Meskel (the Finding of the True Cross).
Autocephalous under its own Patriarch since 1959; Abune Mathias has served since 2013.
Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Church
Became autocephalous in 1993 after Eritrean independence.
Ethiopianism
Its antiquity inspired African Christian independence movements and later Rastafari.
Ethiopian Catholic Church
A Catholic branch of Ge'ez rite separated from it.
Frumentius
First bishop of Aksum, consecrated by Athanasius.
Ezana of Aksum
King who adopted Christianity in the 4th century.
Yared
6th-century composer of Ethiopian sacred chant.
Zara Yaqob
15th-century emperor and church reformer.
Abune Basilios
First Ethiopian-born Patriarch (1959).
About 43.5% of Ethiopia's population declared Orthodox in the 2007 national census; later surveys suggest a lower share.
denomProfiles/armenian-apostolic/tagline: Church of the first Christian nation and of the Armenian people worldwide.
denomProfiles/armenian-apostolic/coreDoc: Holds the miaphysite Christology of Cyril and does not accept the Council of Chalcedon, a position settled at councils of Dvin from 506.
Claims apostolic foundation by Thaddeus and Bartholomew, and national conversion under Gregory the Illuminator.
Accepts the first three Ecumenical Councils and seven sacraments.
Canonised the victims of the 1915 Armenian Genocide as martyrs in 2015.
denomProfiles/armenian-apostolic/focuses: Preservation of Armenian identity, language and culture, especially in the diaspora.
Remembrance of the genocide and survival of Armenian communities.
Patristic and literary heritage, from Mesrop Mashtots to Gregory of Narek.
Ecumenical relations with Catholics and other Orthodox.
denomProfiles/armenian-apostolic/practic: The Badarak (Divine Liturgy) in Classical Armenian, using unleavened bread and unmixed wine.
Celebrates Christmas and Theophany together on 6 January.
Mother See at Holy Etchmiadzin, led by the Catholicos of All Armenians, with a second Catholicosate of Cilicia in Antelias, Lebanon.
Patriarchates in Jerusalem and Constantinople; the madagh (blessed sacrificial meal) and carved khachkar crosses.
Married priests and celibate vardapets (doctors of the church), from whom bishops are chosen.
denomProfiles/armenian-apostolic/influen: The Cilician see continued as a separate catholicosate after 1441.
The alphabet invented by Mesrop Mashtots for Bible translation founded Armenian letters.
denomProfiles/armenian-apostolic/keyFigu: Evangelist of Armenia and first Catholicos.
10th-century mystic poet, declared a Doctor of the Church by Pope Francis in 2015.
denomProfiles/armenian-apostolic/inIndia: A small but historic Armenian community has churches in Kolkata (Holy Nazareth, built 1724) and Chennai (St Mary's, 1772), and the Armenian College and Philanthropic Academy in Kolkata (1821).
denomProfiles/syriac-orthodox/tagline: Antioch's Miaphysite church, keeper of the West Syriac liturgy and the Aramaic heritage.
denomProfiles/syriac-orthodox/coreDoctri: Miaphysite Christology: one incarnate nature of God the Word, united 'without mixture, confusion or separation'.
Accepts the first three ecumenical councils (Nicaea 325, Constantinople 381, Ephesus 431) and rejects Chalcedon (451).
Holy Tradition, the Fathers (especially Ephrem, Severus of Antioch and Jacob of Serugh) and the canons interpret Scripture.
Seven sacraments, with the Eucharist understood as the true body and blood of Christ.
The 1984 common declaration of Patriarch Zakka I Iwas and Pope John Paul II stated that the two churches confess the same faith in Christ despite different formulas.
denomProfiles/syriac-orthodox/focuses/0: Preserving Syriac (Aramaic) language, chant and manuscripts.
denomProfiles/syriac-orthodox/focuses/1: Survival and pastoral care of communities displaced from Turkey, Iraq and Syria.
denomProfiles/syriac-orthodox/focuses/2: Ecumenical dialogue with Catholic, Eastern Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox churches.
denomProfiles/syriac-orthodox/focuses/3: Monastic life, notably at Mor Gabriel (Tur Abdin, founded 397).
denomProfiles/syriac-orthodox/practices/: Divine Liturgy with the Anaphora of St James and many alternative anaphoras, sung in Syriac and local languages.
Daily office from the Shhimo (weekday breviary) and the Fenqitho (festal hymnary).
Strict fasts: Great Lent, the Nineveh fast (three days) and Wednesday and Friday fasts.
Baptism of infants followed at once by chrismation with holy myron and first communion.
Married parish clergy; bishops drawn from the celibate monastic clergy.
denomProfiles/syriac-orthodox/influenced: The Indian church that remains under the Patriarch of Antioch.
Received the West Syriac rite and episcopal succession from Antioch after 1665.
Formed by Syriac Orthodox who entered union with Rome (patriarchate from 1783).
Retains a reformed form of the West Syriac liturgy received from Antioch.
denomProfiles/syriac-orthodox/keyFigures: Patriarch and chief theologian of the anti-Chalcedonian cause
Bishop of Edessa who rebuilt the hierarchy
Maphrian, polymath and author of the Nomocanon
Signed the 1984 Christological declaration with Rome
Leads the church from Damascus through the Syrian war and its aftermath
denomProfiles/syriac-orthodox/inIndia: The Patriarch of Antioch is head of the Jacobite Syrian Christian Church in Kerala, whose Catholicos of India is consecrated by him; this Indian community is far larger than the church's Middle Eastern membership.
